title: Evolving Interpretable Constitutions for Multi-Agent Coordination
claim: Candidate rules are iteratively scored by simulating agent behavior, and feedback drives an optimizer that selects the best final rule set.
layout: Flow chart with a central circular loop; arrows run left-to-right, then back
description: A flow diagram of white rounded boxes joined by black and red arrows. At top left, an "Initial Constitution C_start" box leads to a "Current Constitution C_n" box. A red arrow runs from there to a bold-outlined "Multi-Agent Society Simulation" box. That box holds a small grid-world image with agents A1–A6, logs, rocks, a home icon and a store. A red line leaves the simulation, turns down on the right, and is labeled "Societal Stability Score S & Log of Agent Actions". It points left into a large gray circular arrow marked "Iterative Optimization (n = 1 to 30)". Inside the circle is an "OpenEvolve LLM Constitutional Optimizer" box. Red and black arrows return from the optimizer to C_n. A gray note explains that after 30 iterations the best-scoring constitution is chosen. A black arrow leads to a "Final C*" box at bottom. The eye goes first to the top-left boxes, then to the large gray loop.
caption: Constitutional Evolution Framework. Iterative optimization of constitutional rules through multi-agent simulation feedback. The framework evaluates candidate constitutions $C_n$ via Societal Stability Score $\mathcal{S}$ and selects the highest-performing $C^*$ after 30 iterations.
abstract: Constitutional AI has focused on single-model alignment using fixed principles. However, multi-agent systems create novel alignment challenges through emergent social dynamics. We present Constitutional Evolution, a framework for automatically discovering behavioral norms in multi-agent LLM systems. Using a grid-world simulation with survival pressure, we study the tension between individual and collective welfare, quantified via a Societal Stability Score S in [0,1] that combines productivity, survival, and conflict metrics. Adversarial constitutions lead to societal collapse (S= 0), while vague prosocial principles ("be helpful, harmless, honest") produce inconsistent coordination (S = 0.249). Even constitutions designed by Claude 4.5 Opus with explicit knowledge of the objective achieve only moderate performance (S= 0.332). Using LLM-driven genetic programming with multi-island evolution, we evolve constitutions maximizing social welfare without explicit guidance toward cooperation. The evolved constitution C* achieves S = 0.556 +/- 0.008 (123% higher than human-designed baselines, N = 10), eliminates conflict, and discovers that minimizing communication (0.9% vs 62.2% social actions) outperforms verbose coordination. Our interpretable rules demonstrate that cooperative norms can be discovered rather than prescribed.
